extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction (general readers of 18th-century narrative)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for producing a digressive, conversational narrative voice that stages scenes, reveals character through action, and deliberately leaves space for the reader's imagination. Emphasises rhetorical pacing, vivid physical detail, and a tolerant approach to narrative time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as conversation; leave room for the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "WRITING, when properly managed (as you may be sure I think mine is) is but a different name for conversation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends treating writing like good company conversation: do not 'talk all' or 'think all' for the reader. "The truest respect which you can pay to the reader’s understanding, is to halve this matter amicably, and leave him something to imagine, in his turn, as well as yourself." In practice: give enough to start the scene or idea, then stop and let the reader complete it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite the reader to imagine details (suggestion over exhaustive description)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let the reader imagine then, that Dr. Slop has told his tale—and in what words, and with what aggravations, his fancy chooses;—Let him suppose, that Obadiah has told his tale also..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After sketching the essential facts, purposely hand off further elaboration to the reader's imagination. Use brief prompts or openings rather than exhaustive depiction; allow readers to supply tone, gestures, and rhetorical flourishes in their minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through specific actions and small gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: The text uses small acts (e.g., Uncle Toby catching and releasing a fly; his patient, placid manner) to convey moral character: "This is a part of his moral character."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show rather than tell: embed moral traits and dispositions in concrete, memorable actions and scenes (an unresenting response, a merciful movement). Such episodes serve as durable moral testimony and shape reader sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, precise physical detail for rhetorical and visual effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy, measured description of Corporal Trim's posture (body swayed, bent forwards to an angle of 85 degrees and a half) and the detailed account of Dr. Slop's fall and muddy appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise bodily and visual details (posture, angle, stains, mud) create persuasive imagery useful to painters, orators, and writers. Even if partly humorous or exaggerated, such exactness anchors comedic or dramatic scenes and enhances verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible handling of narrative time and acceptance of digression
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence against hypercritical pedantry about clock-time: the narrator argues that duration comes from the 'train and succession of our ideas' and rejects strict pendulum measurements of narrative moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit narrative compression, expansion, and digression when useful to the associative flow of ideas. Prioritise 'probability' and imaginative coherence over rigid adherence to chronological minutiae; use digressions to develop character, theme, or rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadow and prepare the reader's imagination for scene entrances
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator lists prior actions and journeys (bringing Uncle Toby from Namur, travelling him in a chariot) to "have prepared the reader’s imagination for the entrance of Dr. Slop ... as much, at least ... as a dance, a song, or a concerto between the acts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prime the reader by assembling relevant background and prior incidents before a character's appearance. Preparation renders entrances satisfying and believable; even humorous or digressive preparation heightens dramatic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learned analogy and technical detail to characterise and amuse, but be aware of interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncle Toby's extended fortification discourse (curtins, ravelins, half-moons, horn-works) both reveals his hobby-horse and provides comic contrast with domestic events; the narrator notes such digressions can be brought on by the character's obsessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialised knowledge, technical analogy, and erudite digressions can richly characterise speakers and produce comic effect. However, be mindful they may distract from the immediate plot or anger interlocutors (the narrator's aside about being 'souse into the middle of the old subject'). Use such material to illuminate character while controlling pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulate humour and rhetorical devices (puns, mock-seriousness) to audience and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The father dislikes puns and is provoked by them; the narrator notes that Dennis the critic 'could not detest and abhor a pun' more cordially than the father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour (puns, mock-seriousness) is a stylistic choice that affects tone and reader response. Apply puns and verbal play with awareness of their potential to irritate or undercut serious discourse; let character and context determine whether a pun is appropriate.
